msItem.author: Nicholas de Munshulle (?)
msItem.title: Verbale
msItem.note: Arranged by conjugation and penultimate letter, with principal parts and (usually) English meaning.
msItem.rubric: Verba prime coniugacionis habencia B ante O
msItem.incipit:
labo as bavi batum to slide neutrum
Titulo as aui batum to stumball neutrum
libo as aui atum gustare uel sacrificare actiuum libo degusto liboque sacrifico delibare idem est
msItem.explicit: (fol. 43v) Deponencia quarte coniugacionis ... (fol. 44r) Verba communia quarte coniugacionis. Largior giris gitus sum ri gitum dare uel dari ... Ista sunt verba defectiua ... Bis duo sunt odi noui sepi meminique ... Ista sunt verba anormalatiua que non habent secundam personam ... Sum uolo fert & edo sunt hec anormala credo ... Composita de sum ... Supersum es fui esse to be obowe. Est notat apparat contingat perinet extat Estque nomen domino radix et publica verbum

msItem.author: Nicholas de Munshulle (?)
msItem.title: Nominale
msItem.note: With declension and English meaning, arranged by subject
msItem.incipit: hic deus dei anglice god. Et nota quod deus caret uocatiuo casu secundum vsum & non secundum anologiam. Versus Dat deus ecce dee licet inde faris pharisee ... capitulum de maria amen. Hec maria rie id est genitrix dei o theothecos idem est ... capitulum de angelis. Hic angelus li an angel
msItem.explicit: De nominibus specierum. Hic appotecarius rij specier ... capitulum de lanificio. Hoc lanificium cij wllunwerk ... hoc linarium rij tawrye hoc genethium thij idem est hoc linificium cij tawyng hoc linodium dij flaxe bolle
msItem.note: Ends incomplete in 'capitulum de lanificio'. Fol.44v is blank.

The Nominale and Verbale occur together in Oxford, Trinity College, MS. 14 (N+V) and Lincoln Cathedral, MS. 88 (N+V). MS. Bodl. 604 seems to contain the Nominale and Verbale with an additional section on adjectives (fols. 50v-55v). BL Royal MS 17 C xvii (item 4c) contains the Nominale only; the Nominale in Harvard Law School MS. 43, fols. 16r-42v is, if not the same text, very closely related.
The attribution to the otherwise unknown Nicholas de Munshulle is found only in the Trinity copy of the Nominale.
msItem.bibl: Extracts pr. J. Griffiths, ‘Book Production Terms in Nicholas Munshall’s Nominale’, in C. G. Fisher and K. L. Scott (eds.), Art into Life: Collected Papers from the Kresge Art Museum Medieval Symposia (East Lansing, MI, 1995), pp. 49–71 (Appendices I–II)

msItem.title: Sermon for Easter Day
msItem.incipit:
Christus resurgens ex mortuis iam non moritur mors illi ultra non dominabitur
as this day our Savyour Criste vyctoriously rose from dethe y after yis dethe of hym xal haue dominacion be ye wych blssyd gret presumptuosnes & powyr of our gostly enmy ye fende
msItem.explicit: Thus yan we muste haue perfyte loue & charyte & clannes of owur sowlys and yf so be yat ony man or woman be remembred of ony dedly synne I charge them or they goo to goddes borde to be confessed to god & to hys gostly fathe for they yat ben in dedly synne knowyng them selff so lat them make clene ther concyens for the welleth of ther sowlys
msItem.note: From fol. 72v line 9 the text is largely identical with an Easter sermon found in the collection transmitted principally in BL Harley MS 2247 and Royal MS 18 B XXV (for which see Wells Rev. 11:4061-70, 4279-80 [20]). The sermon also occurs in a macaronic form in CUL MS Gg.6.16 (indexed IMEP 19, Gg.6.16 [4]; ed. Ariane Lainé, A Late Fiteenth-Century Commonplace Book Edited from Cambridge University Library Ms Gg. 6.16 (Brepols, 2019), pp. 119-121). The Middle English sermon is ed. S. Powell, 'A critical edition of the Temporale sermons of MSS Harley 2247 and Royal 18 B XXV' (thesis, University of London, 1980), I.255-260 (sermon 19) with notes at I.487-493. The main variation here is the omission of the paragraph on goats, lines 23-36.

The opening part of our sermon (fols. 71r-72v line 9), which does not appear to be attested elsewhere, also deals principally with the need for confession before communion. People are divided into three conditions, those of Judas, of Peter, and of John. Reference is made to the Easter plague under Gregory I and to the reasons why Easter is called God's own day, and to three kinds of people who receive the sacrament.

msItem.title: Sermon for Easter Day
msItem.incipit: uerans and friends, after the commendabyll costome of holy chyrche thys day ye shall receyue yat precyus body of criste very god body in forme of bredde yat toke flesch & blodde
msItem.explicit: In lyke wyse yf yer war a c Ml. men in a chyrche & one prest saythe masse & yet is not ye masse but on substans yet euery man heryth an holle masse
msItem.note: An Easter sermon found also in the collection transmitted principally in BL Harl. MS. 2247 and Royal MS 18. B. XXV, as above; ed. Powell, thesis, I.273-279; at lines 58-93 our text follows R in discussing how several men can receive the host although there is only one God. Breaks off incomplete (ed. p. 276) due to loss of text after fol. 75.
Rest of fol. 75(b) recto, fol. 75(b) verso, and fol. 75(c) recto blank.

msItem.rubric:
W. Smyth mad to the lorde protector &
kynges honorabyll consell ye ij day of December
yerre of his rengne
msItem.incipit: & wyth mowth I confesse that in ye hygh commonly called the sacrament of ye aulter
msItem.explicit: suffer rather my sowlle from my body to be from this treyth to be separatyd or devydyd
msItem.note: Smith acknowledges transubstantiation and that the mass is a sacrifice. Apparently the same text (otherwise unknown) was listed among the 'unlawful' books seized from John Stow in February 1569: 'A confession of William Smith made to the Lord protectours grace and the rest of the Kinges most honorable Counsell the first of December in the vj yere Domini Edwardi vjth [1552] in wrytten hand.' (Janet Wilson, 'A catalogue of the 'unlawful' books found in John Stow's study on 21 February 1568/9', Recusant History 20 (1990) 1-30 (p. 4)).
Fol. 75(a) is misbound, verso as recto.

msItem.title: Poem attacking Protestant reformers
msItem.rubric: A commendation & exhortacion to his frends wyth his testament
msItem.note: 32 eight-line stanzas and two distichs. Those named include John Lambert (d.1538), Thos. Garrat (d.1540), William Jerome (d.1540), and Thos. Bilney (d.1531).

msItem.author: John Mandeville
msItem.title: Travels
msItem.incipit: (fol. 86r) myche as thay went gyrdelis vndirnethe. Som oþere ar þere þat is clepid Nestorens som Ariens
msItem.explicit: (fol. 89v) Now schull y say to ȝow of her letteres þat thay haue with her names and the manere of her fegureȝ
msItem.note: Fragment of the 'defective version', chs. 8-13 (EETS OS 319 p. 49 line 30 - p. 63 line 23). Placed by Seymour (op. cit. p. xxv) in subgroup 3 (elsewhere called subgroup C); dialect identified by Seymour as 'East Midlands'.

The text is continuous but the leaves misbound, the correct order being 86, 87, 84, 85, 90, 91, 88, 89. Not mentioned in J. W. Bennett The Rediscovery of Sir John Mandeville, New York, 1954, pp.288–297. The text is accompanied by crude marginal drawings in colour, not all related to the text.
